[Soft smile] Good morning—my name is Maya Carter, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I’m so glad you’re here.

Today we’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS. It’s a brief, well-studied set of ten questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s simply a snapshot of your emotional health so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and our team, and we’ll move at whatever pace feels comfortable. I’ll ask each question conversationally—no check-boxes or forms while we talk—and we’ll cover ten areas about the past seven days. If any question feels difficult, we can pause or come back to it.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first one:

Over the past week, when you were able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how often did you feel that laughter came easily to you?

[small smile] Honestly… most of the time, I still laugh pretty easily. Like, when my partner makes a goofy face at the baby or when the dog snores louder than the infant—those things still get me giggling. I’d say I’ve felt that way… yes, most of the days this past week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I’d say that matches how I feel—most days I can still laugh without much effort.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee or taking the baby out in the stroller when the weather’s nice. It’s not every single thing, but most little plans feel good to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if the baby’s fussy and I can’t figure out why, I might think, “Was it something I ate?” for a second—but I don’t stay stuck on it. I shrug it off pretty fast and try the next thing on the list: diaper, feed, cuddle, repeat.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get a little wave of “what-if” sometimes—like I’ll suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing sounds different, even though she looks fine. It’s not all day, just quick flashes a couple of times. Once I check on her and she’s okay, the worry fades.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like that. I haven’t had any sudden scares or panicky feelings—just those quick “is she okay?” checks, but they pass right away.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like yesterday when the laundry pile felt twice as tall as the baby and she wouldn’t nap unless I held her. For a minute I thought, “How am I going to get anything done?” But once she finally settled and I folded a couple onesies, it felt manageable again.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my mood hasn’t messed with my sleep. Once the baby goes down for her first long stretch, I’m out like a light—sometimes I don’t even hear her first little wiggle; my partner has to nudge me.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I get tired, sure, but I wouldn’t call it sad or miserable—more just “end-of-the-day worn out.” When the baby gives me that little milk-drunk smile, I’m right back to feeling fine.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried at all this week. I might feel a little teary when I’m super tired, but the tears never actually come—just a yawn and then I move on.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. That thought hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (partner present), self-report via EPDS-style items

Symptoms / Concerns Reported  
- Mild, transient worries about infant well-being (Q4) – no pervasive anxiety or panic attacks (Q5)  
- Occasional feeling of being overwhelmed, situational (Q6) – resolves with problem-solving/rest  
- No persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep-mood link, crying spells, or self-harm thoughts (Q1–3, 7–10)

Pattern  
- Maintains capacity for pleasure, laughter, and future-oriented enjoyment  
- Rapid rebound from momentary stress; no ruminative self-blame

Screening Significance  
- Current responses do not indicate clinically significant depression or anxiety symptoms  
- No safety concerns identified

Overall Observation  
Screen negative for postpartum depression and anxiety at this time; routine surveillance and psycho-education recommended.
